title: The cost function
html:
Purpose. A computer cannot look at a plot and say "that line looks good". It needs one number that measures how wrong a line is, and the training task becomes making that number small.

Key ideas

  • The cost J(w, b) is the average squared error, with a factor 1/2 that tidies later maths.
  • A lower cost means a better fit, so training means minimizing J.
  • J as a function of w and b is a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the best line.
  • Squared error for linear regression gives a bowl with a single bottom (convex), so there are no traps.

5.1 The formula

J(w,b)=12m∑i=1m(fw,b(x(i))−y(i))2J(w,b) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{w,b}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)^2

Read it from the inside out: the error of example i, squared, added over all m examples, divided by m to get an average (so that the number does not grow just because you have more data), and divided by 2 as well. The extra 2 does nothing to the answer: it only cancels the 2 that appears when you take the derivative in Chapter 6.

5.2 A worked example

Use the three points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) and fix b = 0, so the cost depends only on w. For w = 0.5:

J = 1 / (2 x 3) x ( (0.5 - 1)^2 + (1 - 2)^2 + (1.5 - 3)^2 ) = (0.25 + 1 + 2.25) / 6 = 0.583

w The line Cost J(w)
1 Goes through every point 0
0.5 Too flat 0.583
0 Flat at zero 2.333

Plot cost against w and you get a parabola (a U shape) whose lowest point is at w = 1. The goal of linear regression is to find the w and b that sit at the bottom.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])

def cost(w, b):
    return np.sum((w * x + b - y) ** 2) / (2 * len(x))

print(cost(1, 0), round(cost(0.5, 0), 3), round(cost(0, 0), 3))   # 0.0 0.583 2.333

5.3 Seeing the bowl

With both w and b free, J is a surface over a plane: a bowl, like a soup bowl or a hammock. A contour plot shows the same bowl from above, like a topographic map: every ring is a set of (w, b) pairs with the same cost, and the centre is the minimum. In Ng's housing example a point far from the centre (w about -0.15, b about 800) is a very bad line, while points near the centre fit well. Reading such plots by hand does not scale, so we need an algorithm that walks to the centre by itself. That is gradient descent.

5.4 Convex: one bottom, no traps

The squared-error cost of linear regression is convex: one bowl, one lowest point, no side valleys. Wherever you start, going downhill ends at the global minimum. The cost surface of a neural network is not convex. It has many valleys (local minima), and where training ends depends on where it started.

5.5 Other ways to measure error

Beyond the videos. The squared error is the standard choice, but there are others, and you will meet these names:

Measure Formula in words Notes
MSE (mean squared error) average of the squared errors the cost J without the 1/2: here 2 x 0.583 = 1.167
RMSE square root of the MSE same units as y, so easier to explain: 1.08 here
MAE (mean absolute error) average of the absolute errors treats all errors alike, less hurt by outliers
R squared 1 minus (error around the fit) / (error around the mean) 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always guessing the average

A bank manager understands "typically wrong by 22 euros a month" (RMSE) better than "mean squared error 480".

Loan example. Take the monthly cost of each offer. The cost J measures how far, on average and squared, the predicted monthly cost is from the real one. One outlier offer with a 500 euro error adds as much squared error as 25 offers with a 100 euro error. Check whether that is what you want, because it decides whether MSE or MAE suits the business.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing the cost of two models on different datasets, or one on training and one on test data.
  • Forgetting that the cost depends on the units of y. A cost of 480 is large for prices in dollars and tiny for prices in cents.
  • Believing a low cost proves the model is good. It might simply fit the training data too closely (Chapter 11).

Check yourself

  • Compute J for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) and w = 2, b = 0.
  • Why divide by m? Why divide by 2?
  • What does convex mean, and why is it good news?
Show answers

(1) The line predicts 2 and 4, the errors are 0, so J = 0. (2) Dividing by m makes the cost an average that does not depend on the amount of data; the 2 only cancels the 2 from the derivative. (3) The cost has one bottom and no false valleys, so downhill always ends at the best solution.
